h1: Learning to brew professionally while keeping your day job
title: Learn Pro Brewing, Keep Your Day Job | Craft Beer School
desc: How to build real brewing skills while keeping your day job: weekend study, homebrewing with discipline, brewery shifts and when to make the jump.
teaser: Quitting first and learning later is the expensive way round. There is a slower route that works.
standfirst: Most people who move into brewing do not quit on a Monday and start brewing on Tuesday. They learn in evenings and weekends until the move makes sense. Here is how to do that well.
sections: Why keeping the job makes sense

Brewing jobs are often fewer and lower paid at entry level than people expect. The first role is usually an assistant position with physical work and early starts. Quitting a stable job before you know whether you enjoy that work or whether a brewery will hire you, is a big risk.

Keeping your job while you learn gives you time to test the idea properly. You can find out whether you like cleaning tanks at 7 in the morning as much as you like drinking good beer. You build skills and contacts. When you do move, you move with a plan. Our guide to the move from homebrewer to pro brewer covers the end of this road.

Homebrewing is the cheapest brewing lab you will ever have. Treat it like one. Brew on a schedule, perhaps once or twice a month. Keep proper records: recipe, gravities, temperatures, timings and tasting notes. Change one thing at a time so you learn what each change does.

Measure what a brewery would measure. Check your mash temperature with a calibrated thermometer, take original and final gravity readings and work out your efficiency. A homebrewer who knows their efficiency to within a couple of percent and can explain why it moves is already thinking like a brewer.
Step two: study the science in structured blocks

Books and videos help, but self-study tends to skip the hard parts. A structured course with a fixed schedule makes you learn the biochemistry of mashing, yeast behaviour, hop chemistry and packaging in the right order.

For working people, weekend courses fit best. Two hours on Saturday and Sunday with weekly assignments is manageable alongside a full-time job. Recordings help when a work deadline clashes with a class. Our guide to a brewing degree versus a short course compares the options if you are deciding how deep to go.
Step three: get time in a real brewery

Nothing replaces time on a commercial brewhouse. Ask a local brewpub whether you can help on brew days, at weekends or on your days off. Offer to clean, carry malt and do the dull jobs. Most brewers will teach someone who is reliable and keen.

If you can take a block of leave, a short internship of one or two weeks teaches a lot. Our guide to a brewery internship in India explains how to find one. Be clear about your availability and stick to it. A volunteer who turns up when they say they will is rare and valued.

Learning a new trade alongside a full-time job is tiring. Be realistic. A typical week might include two hours of class on each weekend day, a few hours on assignments, a homebrew session every other weekend and an occasional brewery shift.

That is a lot. Talk to your family about it. Plan around your busiest work periods. Accept that some weeks you will fall behind and catch up later. Six months to a year of steady effort usually tells you whether brewing is right for you.

Signs that you are ready to move:

  • You have brewed regularly for a year or more with good records.
  • You understand the science well enough to explain why a beer went wrong.
  • You have worked shifts in a commercial brewery and still want to do it.
  • A brewer you have worked with would recommend you.
  • You have savings to cover a lower starting salary for a while.

If most of those are true, start applying. If not, keep going. There is no deadline.
Protect the day job while you learn

Be open with your employer if a side interest could look like a conflict, for example if you work for a drinks company. Keep brewing activity outside work hours and away from work equipment. It costs nothing and avoids awkward conversations later.

Your day job may help more than you think. Engineers understand pumps and heat exchangers. Finance people understand cost per litre. Marketers understand brands. Chemists and food technologists understand labs.

Some people never fully leave their careers. They combine skills, for example working in data or quality for a drinks company while brewing on weekends. Others use their background to move into brewery roles that need both skills. Think about what you already know that a brewery would value and build on it.
faqs: Can I learn to brew professionally part time?
Yes. A combination of homebrewing, weekend study and shifts in a local brewery builds real skills without leaving your job. It takes longer but carries much less risk.
How long before I can apply for brewery jobs?
It varies, but a year of regular brewing, study and some commercial experience puts most people in a good position to apply for assistant roles.
Many brewpubs welcome reliable help on brew days, especially for cleaning and heavy jobs. Ask politely and be clear about when you can come.
